To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

preparatory activity of the contrlateral dorsal premotor and supplementary motor areas can predict the type of forthcoming sequential finger movement, while execution-related activity of the broad cortical sensory–motor network, including the contralateral primary motor, parieto-occipital and somatosensory areas, can predict the performed sequential finger movement.

preparatory activity of the contrahemispheric motor areas can predict which of two sequential movements will be executed, and that this prediction is not possible from the execution-related activity of the motor network.

the preparatory activity of the dorsal premotor cortex (dPMc) and supplementary motor area (SMA) could predict which of two sequential finger movements a participant would perform, while the executed movement could not.

the representation of motor sequences and the neural mechanisms of action planning.
how the brain organizes complex sequential finger movements.
the question of how the human brain represents a prepared sequential finger movement.

the brain represents a sequence as a whole during preparation but as individual movements during execution.
the dorsal premotor cortex is a key area in the preparatory activity for a complex sequential finger movements.

the brain prepares and represents a whole sequence of finger movements as a set, rather than individual movements, and that this information is represented by preparatory activity in the higher-order motor regions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the brain prepares the whole sequence as a set in higher-order motor areas and that the sequence information is transferred to the sensory-motor network at a later stage of preparation.

the dorsal premotor cortex, which is known to be involved in the preparation of sequential movements, may play an important role in representing the whole sequential finger movements as a set, whereas the somatosensory cortex may be important in representing the individual finger movements.
the brain prepares the whole sequential movement as a single set of movement.

the preparatory activity in the motor regions, especially the dorsal premotor and supplementary motor area, may be useful for understanding the neural mechanisms of motor planning.
